content.title: Scanning Safely: How to Spot QR-Code Phishing (Quishing)
content.summary: Learn how scammers use QR codes in emails to bypass security filters and how you can spot and report quishing attempts safely.
content.body_markdown:
### A Quick Scan Can Cost You

We all love convenience. Whether ordering lunch, checking in for travel, or picking up a parcel, scanning a QR code with a smartphone has become second nature. But cybercriminals know how routine this habit is, and they are taking advantage of it. We all get tricked sometimes [ORG], especially when a busy day has us rushing through our inbox [S1]. Following our earlier session on invoice and payment fraud—the 2026-11-23 'Phishing Simulation Debrief: Invoice and Payment-Redirect Fraud' [ORG]—let’s look at a rapidly growing technique: QR-code phishing, often called "quishing" [S6].

### What Is Happening?

Phishing remains a primary method attackers use to gain initial access to systems [S5]. Attackers are now embedding QR codes directly into emails, sending millions of these messages every day [S6]. These QR codes direct recipients to malicious websites designed to steal credentials or install malware [S6]. During the first quarter of 2025 alone, over one million phishing attacks were observed globally [S6]. By placing malicious links inside an image instead of plain text, attackers attempt to slip past automated email security filters and push you toward scanning with an unmanaged personal phone [S6].

### Red Flags to Watch For

Scammers frequently disguise quishing messages as routine workplace requests. Be on the lookout for these warning signs:

1. **Physical Security and Badge Updates:** An unexpected email asking you to scan a QR code to update your physical office security access, building pass, or digital badge [ORG].
2. **Urgent Delivery or Shipping Alerts:** Notifications claiming a package cannot be delivered unless you scan a code immediately to confirm details [S8] [ORG].
3. **Travel and Calendar Logistics:** Meeting invites or travel itinerary updates prompting you to scan a code to confirm scheduling or access travel documents [ORG].
4. **Urgent or Pressuring Language:** Messages claiming dire consequences, such as account suspension or missing a crucial record update, if you do not act right away [S8].
5. **Odd Links and Shortened URLs:** When your phone camera previews the code, it shows an unexpected domain, a suspicious shortened link, or misspelled brand names [S8].

### What To Do

- **Pause before you scan:** If an email asks you to scan a QR code to perform a work task, verify the request through an established official portal rather than the code [S1] [S3].
- **Check the preview URL:** Most smartphone cameras display the destination web address before opening it. If the link looks unfamiliar or mistyped, do not tap it [S8].
- **Resist the urge to rush:** Scammers rely on stress and haste [S1]. Take a breath and inspect the context of the email.

### How to Report

Never worry about getting in trouble for making a mistake or asking questions—prompt reporting keeps everyone safe [S1] [S3] [ORG]. If you receive a suspicious QR code or email, please forward it immediately to security@nebulon.example.com [ORG].
key_points: Criminals send millions of quishing emails daily to hide malicious URLs inside QR-code images [S6].
Quishing often disguises itself as physical access updates, package deliveries, or calendar logistics [S8] [ORG].
Always inspect the destination URL preview before opening a link from a QR code [S8].
Report suspicious QR emails promptly to security@nebulon.example.com without fear of blame [S1] [S3] [ORG].
red_flags: Emails asking to scan a QR code for physical security, badges, or facility access.
Package or shipping notifications requiring a QR scan to release a delivery.
Urgent calendar or travel logistics emails prompting you to scan a code.
High-pressure language demanding immediate action to avoid penalties.
Camera previews showing strange, misspelled, or untrusted shortened URLs.
actions: Verify unexpected QR code requests through known internal portals or out-of-band channels.
Check the preview link displayed by your camera before tapping to open a site.
Avoid scanning work-related QR codes with personal devices if they request corporate credentials.
Forward suspicious emails and QR codes to security@nebulon.example.com.
content.report_how: Forward the suspicious email directly to security@nebulon.example.com or use the Report Phish button in your email client.

## How To Report Phishing

If you got a phishing email or text message, report it. The information you give helps fight scammers.

- If you got a phishing **email**, forward it to the Anti-Phishing Working Group at [reportphishing@apwg.org(link sends email)](mailto:reportphishing@apwg.org).
- If you got a phishing **text message**, forward it to SPAM (7726).
- Report the phishing attempt to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
